summary: Defines the Binary extension to IMAP4, which lets a client and server exchange message body data without a MIME content-transfer encoding such as Base64. The server does any decoding and the client gets the raw data. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The IMAP BINARY extension lets a client ask the server for message content after MIME transfer encoding has been removed. It also provides a way to send binary data, including data with zero bytes, through IMAP.

subtitle: IMAP can return decoded message data directly, including binary content that contains zero bytes.

tldr.problem: MIME encodings can add substantial overhead when mail content must travel over transports that cannot carry binary data directly.
tldr.mechanism: The BINARY extension adds FETCH items that return decoded content and a literal8 form for transparent eight-bit data. APPEND can also accept literal8 data.
tldr.outcome: Clients can request server-side content-transfer decoding, but the RFC recommends that they remain able to decode content themselves. RFC 3516 is updated by RFC 4466.

today: RFC 3516 is a Proposed Standard, published in April 2003, and is updated by RFC 4466. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Decode Content at the Server
sections.content:
MIME uses content-transfer encodings to carry non-text content over transports that may not pass binary data unchanged. These encodings can add considerable overhead in settings such as slow radio links or streaming multimedia.

The Binary extension lets an IMAP server remove a body's content-transfer encoding before it sends the data to a client. The extension also handles data domains that base IMAP cannot express, such as binary content containing NUL octets.
sections.plainLanguage: MIME encoding can make message content larger. With this extension, the server can remove that encoding before returning the content to the mail client.

sections.title: Decoding and Literal8 Data
sections.content:
Each IMAP body section has a content-transfer encoding (CTE); a section without an explicit header is treated as 7bit. A CTE describes both a decoding method and the kind of data that results. Even when no decoding is needed, the resulting data may not fit the base IMAP string rules.

For those cases, the extension defines literal8, an eight-bit-transparent literal that can carry any octet value. The server first decodes the section when needed, then chooses an IMAP response element that can carry the decoded data.
sections.plainLanguage: The server first removes any required encoding, then checks what form of data remains. Literal8 lets IMAP carry every byte value when ordinary strings cannot.

sections.title: BINARY FETCH Items and Responses
sections.content:
A supporting server MUST advertise BINARY in its CAPABILITY response. Clients can request a decoded body section with BINARY, use BINARY.PEEK without implicitly setting \Seen, or request its decoded size with BINARY.SIZE. For partial requests, offsets refer to the decoded data.

The returned data is an nstring or literal8. If the server cannot decode the CTE, it MUST return NO with the UNKNOWN-CTE response code. The size from BINARY.SIZE MUST equal the size returned by the matching BINARY request; calculating it may be expensive for a server.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can request decoded content, preview it without marking it seen, or ask how large it will be. If the server cannot decode it, the server reports UNKNOWN-CTE.

sections.title: Appending Binary Content
sections.content:
The extension changes APPEND so a client can upload data containing NUL octets by using the literal8 syntax. A server MAY change the content-transfer encoding of the appended data, but that change MUST NOT lose data.

If the destination mailbox cannot store binary content, the server MUST fail the request with a NO response containing UNKNOWN-CTE. The RFC warns that servers should change encodings only when necessary because gratuitous changes can invalidate cryptographic operations on a message.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can append raw binary data, including zero bytes. The server may change its encoding only if no data is lost.

sections.title: Headers, Line Endings and Client Support
sections.content:
The extension decodes message bodies, not MIME-encoded header text. A server MUST NOT convert encoded header text in response to BINARY FETCH or APPEND. It MUST send text sections with IMAP's CRLF line endings, whatever line endings the server used internally.

A server may store binary content without encoding it, but its BODYSTRUCTURE response must still describe it as if it used a CTE accepted by base IMAP. FETCH BODY must return content matching that description. The extension is an optimization; clients SHOULD still be ready to decode CTEs themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: This extension changes body handling, not encoded text in message headers. Clients should keep their own decoding ability in case a server cannot use the extension.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 3516 states that the extension has no known additional security issues beyond those in the base IMAP4rev1 protocol. It warns that changing a message's content-transfer encoding without need can make most cryptographic operations on that message useless.

The extension does not replace the base protocol's security mechanisms. Its requirements preserve message data when a server changes an encoding and leave header encodings untouched.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC identifies no new security issue beyond base IMAP. Unnecessary encoding changes can still break cryptographic operations on a message.
